title: Studio backdrop and three-point lighting
description: Build a curved studio backdrop for the Airline Chair, light it with three area lights in a three-point setup, and make test renders in Cycles to see how sampling trades noise for render time.
content:
A product shot needs a studio: a floor that curves up into a back wall so there's no horizon line behind the object, and lights you place yourself. In this part you'll build that backdrop around the Airline Chair, choose the camera you'll render through, light the chair with three area lights in a three-point setup, and make two test renders in Cycles to see how the sampling level changes the noise and the render time. You'll need your textured Airline Chair from the Texturing the Airline Chair series. The video uses Blender 2.83.

Build the backdrop

  1. Add a large floor. 0:08 Press Shift A and choose Mesh › Plane, then press S and scale it up into a really large floor.

  2. Extrude a back wall. 0:18 Press Tab for Edit Mode and 2 for edge select mode, select the back edge, and extrude it upwards, pressing Z to keep it on the Z axis. You now have a large floor and a large wall.

  3. Bevel the crease. 0:33 Instead of a hard crease where the floor meets the wall, make a smooth curve. Press T to show the toolbar if it's hidden, choose the Bevel tool and drag a bevel out of the edge. At first it makes only one bevel face, so raise Segments in the Bevel panel 0:54 until the curve looks smooth.

  4. Shade it smooth. 1:04 Go back to the Select tool and click anywhere, then press Tab to leave Edit Mode. The curve looks faceted, which is not how it should render, so right-click and choose Shade Smooth. That's your backdrop and floor.

  5. Sit the chair on the floor. 1:24 With the chair in the scene, it's a little below the floor, so move the whole floor down. Select the plane, press G Z and move it down to the bottom of the chair 1:38. Wireframe mode makes the plane easier to see 1:52; zoom in and get it as close as you can. Don't leave the chair hovering above the floor, because sometimes you can tell. It can intersect a tiny bit, but be as precise as you can.

Choose the render camera

  1. Add a camera if you need one. 2:24 Press Shift A and choose Camera; it appears in the Outliner. The video already has a camera set up, so it deletes the new one. If you have a lot of cameras, rename them so you know which is which.

  2. Make it the scene's camera. 2:52 The button that looks through the camera uses the scene's camera. To choose it, open the Scene properties tab (its icon looks like a cone and a sphere) and set Camera at the top: clear the field, then use the eyedropper or click in the field and pick your camera.

  3. Select the camera. 3:31 Click it in the Outliner or, while you're looking through it, click the dotted outline of the camera's frame in the viewport. Its settings are in the camera properties; this part leaves them for later.

Light the chair

  1. Render with Cycles. 3:58 Switch the viewport to rendered shading. Depending on your settings, the render engine may be Eevee, Blender's real-time renderer: it does a pretty good job but needs some configuration to look good. Use Cycles instead (in the Render properties, Render Engine). It takes longer to render because it isn't real time, but the renders typically look better.

  2. Turn off the default light. 4:31 A new scene has a default point light. The video disables it (you can delete it instead) and adds its own lights.

  3. Add an area light for the key light. 4:51 Press Shift A and choose Light › Area: an area light gives a nice soft light. Press G Z to move it up, turn on the rotation handles and rotate it, and move it off to the front so light comes from the front 5:08. This is the key light, your strongest, brightest light. Press S to scale it up, which enlarges the area the light comes from 5:38.

  4. Duplicate it for the fill light. 5:43 A three-point setup, the kind you'll find in studio lighting for products or portraits, has lights in three key places. Press Shift D to duplicate the key light, move the copy to the other side and rotate it towards the chair. This fill light contributes less light to the scene; the key light is much brighter.

  5. Set each light's power. 6:13 With a light selected, open its settings under the light bulb tab and change Power. The video starts by changing 10 W to 100 W, then sets the fill light to 80 W and the key light to 500 W. This takes trial and error: the right power depends on the scale of your scene, so you may need more or less.

  6. Duplicate again for the rim light. 6:56 Duplicate a light, move it behind the chair and rotate it to point at the chair. This is a rim light, or a hair light: in portrait photography it highlights hair, and on an object it makes a rim of light that adds contrast between the object and its background. So the setup has a key light; a fill light, which fills the shadows with a bit of light (a reflector can do that job instead of a light); and a rim light at the back.

Frame the shot

  1. Turn the backdrop. 7:47 To get the backdrop behind the chair in the camera view, rotate the backdrop. You could rotate the chair instead, but here it's easier to rotate the background.

  2. Lock the camera to the view. 8:02 To zoom and move the camera as you would the viewport, open the sidebar's View tab and check Lock Camera to View under View Lock. While it's unchecked, you can't zoom, rotate or move the render camera from the viewport.

Make a test render

  1. Check the resolution. 8:43 Render › Render Image uses the scene's render settings. In the Output properties (the printer icon), check the resolution. The video's file had a wide resolution set for a website banner; set something more like 1920 × 1080.

  2. Render. 9:22 Render a first time to see whether you like the composition and whether the quality is good enough: Render › Render Image. A new window opens, and Cycles renders the image in tiles. This can take a few minutes, depending on your computer; if you have a GPU that Blender supports, you can configure Blender to use it and render faster.

  3. Render again at a lower sampling level. 10:06 To compare, change the slot at the top of the render window to Slot 2 so the first render stays in Slot 1. Then in the Render properties (the camera icon), under Sampling, the video's Render value is 250 (yours may say 128). Lower it to 72 10:41, only slightly higher than the viewport's sampling, and render again. It renders much faster.

  4. Compare the two. 11:12 Zoom in on both renders and look at the shadows. Slot 1, at 250 samples, took over two minutes to render; slot 2, at 72, took 37 seconds. More samples take longer, but they do a better job of reducing noise, and the render is more accurate.

  5. Balance noise against time. 11:54 With Cycles, you're balancing how much noise there is against how long the render takes. This is a fairly simple render and two minutes isn't long to wait, so you could raise the samples from 250 to 500 or 700 to reduce the noise further, and it would take much longer. For this render, viewed from this distance, 250 is pretty good, but 72 isn't enough: it's grainy and not an attractive render. Anything above 200 gives a decent render of this kind; look at your results to decide.

Wrap-up

You've built a seamless backdrop, set the chair on it, chosen the render camera, and lit the chair with a key light, a fill light and a rim light. Your test renders show the trade-off at the heart of Cycles: more samples mean less noise and longer renders. In the next part you'll adjust the lighting to make the render more pleasing.
